name: Topological Sort and Dependency Ordering
intent: Turn a set of tasks with 'must come after' constraints into a valid order in time proportional to tasks plus dependencies, detect a cycle instead of looping on it, and read the parallel schedule (levels) off the same computation.
scenario: A build has 1,000 tasks and 1,523 dependencies between them. A first version picks the next ready task by rescanning the whole list and spends 757,544 operations; Kahn's algorithm does the same job in 5,046. Then someone adds one dependency that closes a 3-task cycle and 465 tasks can no longer be ordered. Finally the team adds workers and finds that 16 of them finish no faster than 1,000 would.
problem: Package installs, build graphs, database migrations, spreadsheet recalculation, CI pipelines and data-pipeline DAGs all have the same shape: some things must happen before others. The order is not unique and not obvious, a hand-written loop that looks for 'anything ready' quietly costs the square of the number of tasks, and one bad dependency makes the problem unsolvable. A good answer must run in linear time, say clearly when no order exists and which tasks are involved, and tell you how much of the work can run in parallel.

howItWorks.title: Model it as a directed graph and ask for an order
howItWorks.text: Each task is a node and each 'B needs A' is an edge from A to B. A topological order lists every node after all the nodes it depends on. One exists exactly when the graph has no cycle, and when it exists there are usually many valid ones: any task whose dependencies are done may come next, so ties are broken by a rule you choose (id, name, declared order). Make that rule explicit if two machines must produce the same order.

howItWorks.title: Kahn: count unfinished dependencies and release at zero
howItWorks.text: Compute for every task how many dependencies it still waits for. Put the tasks with zero in a queue. Take one out, append it to the order, and for each task that depends on it subtract one; any task that reaches zero joins the queue. Every task enters and leaves the queue once and every dependency is looked at once, so the work is proportional to tasks plus dependencies: 5,046 operations for 1,000 tasks and 1,523 dependencies, against 757,544 for the rescanning loop.

howItWorks.title: DFS: finish the dependencies first, then the task
howItWorks.text: Depth-first search visits a task, visits each of its dependencies first, and appends the task when they are all finished. The output order is a valid build order. Colour the nodes: not seen, on the current path, finished. Reaching a node that is on the current path means a cycle, and the path from that node back to itself is the cycle itself, which is a better error message than a count. The cost is also tasks plus dependencies (3,523 operations here), but a very long chain means deep recursion, so a stack overflow is possible on huge graphs unless the search is written with an explicit stack.

howItWorks.title: A cycle has no order: report it, do not guess
howItWorks.text: If Kahn's queue empties before every task is ordered, the tasks left over are in a cycle or depend on one. Adding one 3-task cycle to the 1,000-task build leaves 465 tasks unordered, because everything downstream of the cycle also waits forever. The unordered list is a symptom, not the cycle. Run a DFS on the leftovers to extract an actual cycle path, print it, and fail the build. Dropping an edge silently so that something runs hides a real design error, and some tools do exactly that with only a warning.

howItWorks.title: Read parallelism off the levels
howItWorks.text: Give a task level 1 if it has no dependencies, otherwise one more than the highest level among its dependencies. Tasks on the same level can run at the same time, and the number of levels is the length of the longest chain: the critical path. With unit-time tasks, 394 levels means no number of workers finishes this build in fewer than 394 steps. Four workers need 400, sixteen need 394, and an unlimited number need 394: past a point extra workers are wasted, and only shortening the longest chain helps.

pros: Linear in tasks plus dependencies, so a graph of a million tasks is routine
Detects impossible requirements instead of running forever or producing a wrong order
The same pass yields levels, which show what can run in parallel and what the critical path is
Easy to make deterministic by fixing the tie-break rule, which gives reproducible builds
cons: A valid order is not unique, so results can differ between runs or tools unless the tie-break is fixed
The order says what is allowed, not what is fast: it ignores task duration, so the longest-chain-by-time can differ from the longest-chain-by-count
On a cycle it gives no answer by itself; finding and explaining the cycle needs an extra search
Dependencies must be declared completely: a missing edge gives a valid order that still breaks at run time
whenToUse: Build systems, package installers, migrations and CI jobs where steps declare what they need
Scheduling a data pipeline or workflow DAG and deciding which stages can run side by side
Evaluating formulas or derived values that refer to each other, such as spreadsheet cells or configuration with references
Validating that a set of declared dependencies is consistent before a long run starts
whenNotToUse: The constraints are not simple precedence (for example 'at most 2 of these at once' or 'these two must not overlap'): that needs a scheduler or a solver on top of, or instead of, the ordering
The graph legitimately contains cycles, such as mutual references that are resolved by iteration until values settle: collapse the strongly connected components first or use a fixed-point method
There are a handful of tasks and the order is obvious: write them in order
Order does not matter and everything is independent: just run them in parallel
pitfalls: Rescanning for 'the next ready task' after every pick: it looks harmless and costs the square of the task count (757,544 operations against 5,046 at 1,000 tasks, and the gap widens with n). Keep a queue of ready tasks instead

Having no cycle check: a loop that waits for 'something ready' never ends on a cycle; a DFS that only marks nodes as seen, without the on-path colour, finishes but silently returns an order that breaks a dependency, and one with no marking at all recurses until the stack overflows. Check explicitly and fail with the cycle
Reading 'N tasks could not be ordered' as 'N tasks are in a cycle': in the example only 3 tasks form the cycle and 465 are stuck, because everything that depends on them is stuck as well
Silently breaking a cycle to keep going: the build may pass today and ship a wrong result, because an ordering that ignores a real dependency can run a task before its input exists
Assuming more workers always help: the number of levels is a floor (394 here), and 16 workers were already at it. Look at the critical path before buying capacity
Depending on the incidental order: many valid orders exist, so code that works only in the order your tool happened to print is a latent bug. Declare the dependency instead
Forgetting transitive and implicit dependencies, such as a generated file or a shared resource: the sort is exactly as correct as the edges you gave it

roles.label: Dependency graph
roles.description: Holds the tasks and the 'needs' edges between them.

roles.label: Ready queue
roles.description: Tasks whose dependencies are all finished, waiting to be taken.

roles.label: Build order
roles.description: The output: every task after everything it depends on.

roles.label: Workers
roles.description: Run the tasks of one level at the same time.

quiz.question: Kahn's algorithm orders 535 of 1,000 tasks and stops, although only 3 tasks form a cycle. Why are 465 tasks left?
options: The queue ran out of memory after 535 tasks and the rest were dropped.
Tasks that depend on a cycle, directly or not, never reach zero unfinished dependencies.
Kahn handles at most 535 tasks per pass, so a second run is needed.
Another 462 tasks form other cycles that the algorithm silently broke.
quiz.explanation: A task is released only when all of its dependencies are finished. The 3 cycle tasks wait for each other forever, and every task downstream of them waits too. The leftover count is a symptom; a DFS over the leftovers finds the actual cycle to report.

quiz.question: A build has 394 levels. Four workers need 400 steps and sixteen need 394. What do you get from an unlimited number of workers?
options: About 100 steps, since the work is spread over more workers.
Fewer than 394 steps, once the scheduler stops being the limit.
Exactly 1,000 steps, because the order is fixed by the sort.
394 steps, since the longest chain of dependent tasks must run one after another.
quiz.explanation: Tasks in a chain cannot overlap, so the number of levels is a floor on the finish time. Once the workers cover the widest level the build is already at that floor. Only splitting or removing links in the longest chain makes it faster.

quiz.question: Why does the rescan-for-the-next-ready-task loop cost 757,544 operations at 1,000 tasks while Kahn costs 5,046?
options: It restarts the scan after every pick, so total work grows with the square of the task count.
It checks dependencies twice, which doubles the cost of each task.
It uses recursion, and every call copies the whole graph.
It sorts the tasks by name before each pick, which takes time proportional to n log n.
quiz.explanation: Each of the n picks scans up to n tasks to find a ready one, so the work is about n squared, while the queue gives Kahn the next ready task in constant time. The gap is a factor of about 150 at 1,000 tasks and grows with n.
